stories.body:
About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border

After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.

Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.

Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.

At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.

According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.

Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.

“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.

Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.

“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”

“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”

Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.

The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet , which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”

At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.

The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.

Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.

She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”

She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”

Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.

According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

stories.body:
Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls

China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.

The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.

China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air .

The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February .

How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.

The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.

This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence.

In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.

after newsletter promotion

Analysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” said Lauri Myllyvirta , the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”

Myllyvirta noted this was the first time China’s overall emissions had fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.

In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.

Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst at Ember , which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.

“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”

stories.title: Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
stories.summary: Andy Burnham has committed to reaching the Nato target of 3.5% spending by 2035, but not 3% by 2030.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch giving a speech on defence

Published 3 September 2026, 14:20 BST

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused the prime minister of "kicking defence spending into the long grass" as she set out Tory plans to push the figure to 3% of GDP by 2030.

Badenoch said a Conservative government would fund the commitment, worth £10bn a year, through measures including reimposing the two-child benefit cap, reforming housing benefit and ending VAT exemptions for Motability cars.

Pointing to the threat from countries like Russia and Iran, Badenoch told a press conference: "Conflict is coming, we must act now."

So far Andy Burnham's government has only committed to setting out a plan in the spring to meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.

Speaking at an event in central London, Badenoch said: "Andy Burnham is kicking defence spending into the long grass.

"Our enemies are not going to sit around and wait for Labour to find the money to fight them."

Burnham has pointed to his choice of Chancellor, John Healey, who quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, as proof of his commitment to defence investment.

However, Badenoch said the prime minister should call a general election if he is not willing to find the money now, adding that Healey's decision to quit over defence spending appeared to have changed since he became chancellor.

"He resigned because Britain was not on track to reach 3% by 2030 and I praised him at the time for that decision," she said.

"Now that he is chancellor he does not seem to believe that any more and I am concerned he has been bought off with a promotion."

Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge Published 22 hours ago

Badenoch accuses Starmer of leaving defence spending 'mess' for Burnham Published 1 July

Starmer dithering over defence spending, says Badenoch Published 10 June

Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.

The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April , meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.

She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.

The Tories said this would include saving at least £4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving £1bn.

"Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.

Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with £37.3bn forecast to be spent.

The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.

Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.

Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this.

"It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC.

"Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era.

"Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe.

"In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."

It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.

Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.

Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.

stories.title: Trump hints US would not back UK over Falkland Islands due to lack of Iran war support
stories.summary: The US president says the UK was not "there to help me" in his ongoing war with Iran.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Previous US administrations have taken a neutral position on the islands' sovereignty

Published 3 hours ago

Donald Trump has hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.

In an interview with GB News, the US president said that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran, despite later saying his military did not need any support.

Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.

Argentinian President Javier Milei is due to make a televised statement on Thursday night about what he describes as his nation's "historic" claim to the islands.

The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory.

When asked if he would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump told GB News: "Well look, I was there when they had the first war.

"That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away."

Turning his attention to the US' current conflict with Iran, he added: "So, your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me.

"Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?'

Trump said the-then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, told him no vessels were available, which "was pretty sad", he added.

He also said: "Nato was not there, even though they get – most of those countries get – a big portion of their oil from there. So we're doing that by ourselves".

Argentina and the UK waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

Seventy-four days of fighting led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Trump's comments come after he was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the islands .

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

Watch: Andy Burnham and Emmanuel Macron shake hands outside No 10

Published 3 September 2026, 12:24 BST

Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron have discussed how to "scale up" efforts to tackle illegal migration and move the UK closer to Europe, as the new prime minister hosted his first foreign leader in Downing Street.

In an official readout of their meeting, No 10 said the pair also discussed production of long-range missiles in Ukraine.

Meanwhile, the prime minister raised Israeli plans for new settlements in the West Bank , which he condemned as "unacceptable".

Burnham said it was "so fitting" that Macron was his first overseas visitor since becoming PM in July, describing him as "our nearest neighbour and close friend Emmanuel".

"It shows what collaboration can achieve, just as we are also showing on Ukraine, on small boats, and also on strengthening the UK-EU relationship," Burnham added.

Macron and Burnham held talks on a range of issues

Macron said: "This is a very strong relationship. For me it is extremely important, and I'm here with willingness and a commitment to get closer."

The French leader's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum . He met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.

In bilateral talks on Thursday, No 10 said Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

They also "discussed the UK's drive to get closer to Europe", while Burnham raised concerns about the potential impact of the Made in Europe procurement plan, being drawn up in Brussels to protect EU industries, on British sectors.

Burnham has previously called for closer ties with Europe, as had his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The pair also discussed establishing local assembly lines in Ukraine for the Scalp long-range missile , a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile.

The leaders also discussed the situation in the Middle East and the need to ensure de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz.

And Burnham raised Israel's move to open up tenders for the construction of settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank , saying it was "unacceptable and only served to undermine the prospect of the two-state solution".

The development in the so-called E1 area would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Plans to build there have long been internationally condemned, with settlements illegal under international law.

The arrival of the first foreign leader under the Burnham premiership is an important symbolic moment - it shows the relationship with Paris is an important priority.

But it also reflects an obvious reality - to further reduce small boats crossings, working with France will be essential.

France and the UK have been working extremely closely on Ukraine and Iran, trying to jointly influence the White House.

And Paris will be an important player as the UK seeks even stronger economic ties with Europe under the new No 10 administration.

The "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.

It follows a summer when the number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.

Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16,513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 2 September 2025 to 1 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

Earlier on Tuesday, Home Office Minister Anna Turley said the officers were "just part of the armoury" of more than 1,000 officers on northern French beaches who are now doing "actual intervention" in the water.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that videos in recent weeks "show them going to the boats, slashing them, pushing people back, being bombarded with stones and bricks and coming under a lot of challenge to do that, so they are intervening".

In a post on X , external , in which he said he was "do[ing] politics differently", Burnham laid out the latest small boat, returns and asylum hotel figures, describing smuggling gangs as a "shared European challenge".

Asked about the extra police on French beaches, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC she welcomed European collaboration "but the boats aren't stopping".

"We have spent hundreds of millions, if not billions, paying the French to man the borders," she said.

stories.body:
Bank says gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily and the move will allow it to respond more rapidly in a ‘crisis situation’

The Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US and Canada to London, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest”.

De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) said gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily than those held in New York and Ottawa.

“This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” the bank said in a statement on Wednesday.

“With this step, we have improved the deployability of the gold reserves. We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” said DNB’s president, Olaf Sleijpen.

The total Dutch gold stock amounted to 612.4 tonnes and was valued at €72.2bn ($83.7bn) at the end of 2025, said the DNB.

Before the deployment, the Dutch bank held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa.

After the move, each country accounted for 18.5% of the Dutch gold reserve.

The share of gold held in London increased from 18.1% to 32.1%. The bank still holds 30.8% of its gold in the Netherlands .

The transfer was carried out partially by buying and selling and partly by physically transferring gold, the bank said.

The bank moved more than 27 tonnes of physical gold from the US and Canada to Zeist.

The same quantity of gold was moved from Zeist to London, preventing the melting down of gold bars.

“By combining buying and selling and physical transport, the risks associated with physically moving a large quantity of gold have been spread,” the DNB said.

The operation took place between March and August of this year, it said.

Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based National Gold Counter, which facilitates gold trading in France, said central banks had been moving their reserves around for about a decade.

“The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations,” he said.

The London market was the deepest and most liquid, Schwartz said, making it easier to deploy in times of crisis.

“Central banks can more easily lend their gold there to other banking institutions.”

John Plassard, an analyst at Cite Gestion Private Bank, said the Dutch move was intended “for there to be more immediate availability in the event of a crisis”.

For the moment, it was a “fairly one-off move”, but he warned that if other central banks followed suit, it could damage confidence in the US.

At the beginning of the year, there were concerns raised in Germany about the security of its central bank’s reserves in New York.

However, the powerful Bundesbank has decided for the moment not to shift its reserves away from New York.

“The New York Fed is and remains an important storage site for our gold,” the bank told public TV station ARD in January.

stories.summary: Cold War veterans who oversaw nuclear tests have claimed they caused lifelong health problems.

Watch: 'Absolute cover-up' on nuclear test veterans' medical records, Ellwood says

Published 3 September 2026, 07:52 BST

Former veterans minister Tobias Ellwood has accused the Ministry of Defence (MoD) of deliberately withholding the medical records of Cold War veterans who oversaw nuclear tests, calling it "an absolute cover-up".

Ellwood told BBC Newsnight he now believes some information he gave to Parliament about the UK's nuclear programme, based on MoD briefings, was "a complete lie".

Veterans have campaigned for the release of their medical histories, arguing blood and urine test results could help them prove that nuclear exposure damaged their health.

An MoD spokesperson said the government had conducted an "extensive records discovery exercise" to address questions about the programme, with its findings published in full.

As many as 25,000 members of the UK armed services, scientists and civilians took part in the nuclear testing programme between 1952 and 1967 at sites including Australia and several islands in the Pacific Ocean.

Veterans have claimed the tests caused severe lifelong health problems, alleging they have suffered cancers of the liver, bone, bowel, skin and brain, as well as leukaemia, heart disease, stillbirths and generational birth defects as a result of their exposure.

Ellwood, who served as a junior defence minister between June 2017 and July 2019, said he believed ministers over the years had been briefed to say they had no evidence to help nuclear test veterans, despite thousands of documents about the programme being held.

He said the information was "deliberately withheld" by the MoD and claimed there was an effort to delay its release until surviving veterans had passed away.

"The more you unpick this story, the more murky, the more shady, the concerning it becomes," Ellwood told Newsnight, calling it bigger than the infected blood, Windrush and Post Office scandals "because of the longevity... and the number of people that have been involved".

"This is a scandal. It's absolutely tarnished the reputation of the MoD."

Calling for an independent tribunal into the matter, Ellwood asked: "Why it is that the MoD - rather than help veterans, provide the information - closed ranks and said 'nothing to see here', and then told ministers such as me 'actually we haven't got that information and we're not willing to help the veterans'?"

The ministry in 2024 promised to embark on a comprehensive examination of any information the department held on the issue, and has since released five reports.

In those, it said there were a number of factors affecting the way medical records were kept, including the lack of a centralised approach and high levels of Cold War "secrecy".

Ellwood conceded that some documents were to be handed to the National Archives, but said they would still be heavily redacted: "They have to be declassified. This isn't enough to help the veterans, who understandably remain deeply angry."

An MoD spokesperson said the government had examined "tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme".

They said it had been published in its entirety "following regular engagement between Ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process."

"We owe an enduring debt of gratitude to the more than 22,000 Service personnel, scientists and civilians who contributed to the UK's nuclear testing programme and helped safeguard our national security," the spokesperson said.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
stories.summary: The party's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny, says BBC political editor Chris Mason.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 3 September 2026, 02:55 BST

Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in the Senedd and in local authorities.

But they also gather amid significant political headwinds, much of which revolve around money.

There was that whopping £5m gift to Nigel Farage from Christopher Harborne, the Thailand based British billionaire, and the long running row about whether the money should have been declared by Farage once he became an MP.

Then there is, among other things, the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to the party during the last general election campaign.

Reform insists that it "takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations."

When the party got together in the same West Midlands venue a year ago, they were an insurgency provoking intrigue and attention and demonstrating plenty of momentum.

Indeed that momentum was so significant that it was a major factor, perhaps the major factor, in accelerating the demise of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, because the potential prospect of a Reform government frightened the Labour Party to its core.

Would Starmer, its then desperately unpopular leader, help or hinder their attempts to take on Farage? Hinder was the eventually overwhelming view within Labour, and so Starmer was a goner.

But politics can change, and change quickly. With Starmer out and Burnham in, there is early evidence of some support for Labour picking up. No longer are Reform comfortably leading in all the opinion polls - in some they're not leading at all. Add to this a more confident and prominent Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives and the recent rise too of Restore Britain, the outfit set up by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. And the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru won and so beat them in the devolved elections in Scotland and Wales respectively. In other words, collectively Reform's opponents appear more energised and popular.

Make no mistake, no party at a UK wide level is popular at the moment, but the scrap appears more evenly matched than it did.

This video can not be played

Watch: 'I firmly believe I have broken no rules,' Farage tells BBC

Into that mix, Reform's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny. Nigel Farage is a candidate for prime minister; his senior team candidates for the great offices of state.

When I interviewed Farage at Reform HQ yesterday, on the specifics of the £5m gift and the police investigation he maintained they've acted appropriately.

But he offered an insight into how he perceives the hurricane of questions he faces.

"I think what you're seeing is the establishment - in a very coordinated way - fighting back," he claimed.

I suggested he sounded like a conspiracy theorist, implying the whole world was out to get him.

His answer was instructive: "When you read in the newspaper you're under investigation, and you don't even know a complaint's been made, you can see the degree of collusion that has gone on between interested parties. This will not stop. They will continually try and do this to us."

Who's they? I pressed. He mentioned the House of Commons and House of Lords – full of his political opponents – but didn't name anyone or anything else.

"I'm talking about normal human behaviour. People who, people who hold positions of power, influence, and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding."

Let's be clear – it is a big claim to allege collusion between institutions or organisations collectively seeking to undermine him and his party, and there is no evidence for it.

But, crucially, you hear in his answer a sense of why he perceives that - that is what it feels like.

The question, as Reform's conference gets under way, is how the party approaches the coming days and the coming months.

Will Nigel Farage ditch the "aggrieved" tone he has been accused of adopting recently?

Reform up against 'complainants' society', Farage tells BBC Published 1 day ago

Yes, his clear hint to me.

"I've generally, you know, gone through politics with a smile…I'll go back to doing what I've been doing for the last 34 years," he said.

And as for their pitch to you at conference? A Reform government would achieve, and achieve quickly, they claim.

The party is promising a list of promises it would deliver in the first 100 days of a majority government, with every senior minister in a Farage government making and delivering one clear pledge.

But would they be able to if there is validity in their current claim that plenty of institutions are trying to stymie them?

Japan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieve

“I n the midst of every crisis lies great opportunity” is an aphorism attributed to Albert Einstein . It seems to be taken to heart by this White House. A global bond sell-off sparked by an inflationary shock emanating from the Gulf sees Donald Trump seeking to restrict plans by Japan – a longtime ally – to reduce dependence on an international system America dominates.

Japan, a successful exporter, has long done things its own way. For years Tokyo saw off the bond vigilantes despite running enormous deficits and a huge national debt. It demonstrated how a central bank could fund public spending and keep interest rates low if it wanted to. This economic model was refined by Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister. However, this week the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent , called time on Abenomics as his price for US help in stabilising Japan’s currency. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, he indicated, should shrink her $2tn spending plans and raise rates. Abenomics did not suddenly become financially impossible. It became inconvenient to the issuer of the world’s reserve currency.

Kevin Warsh, Mr Trump’s handpicked chair of the US Federal Reserve, has made it clear that he will raise interest rates in response to inflationary pressures. Others will be expected to follow. In Japan’s case, Washington fears that a yen crisis could become a bond crisis. A disorderly rout could force Japan into ever larger currency interventions – and repeated appeals to Washington to help defend the yen. If such aid proved inadequate, Tokyo could end up defending its currency by dumping US treasury bonds – of which it has more than a trillion dollars worth – and put upward pressure on the very yields Mr Bessent is trying to contain. His demand that Tokyo raise rates and cut spending is not just about Japanese inflation. It is about trying to prevent Tokyo’s adjustment to the Iran shock being exported on to America’s balance sheet.

Mr Burnham’s first Commons speech as prime minister suggests an expansive programme to raise living standards and get growth through regional reindustrialisation. This, he says, rests on the “bedrock” of fiscal responsibility. Mr Burnham promises an activist state to deal with four decades of underinvestment and privatisation. But retaining Rachel Reeves’s fiscal framework leaves his investment plans hostage to interest rates, debt costs and feverish “ headroom ” speculation. Turmoil in global bond markets could derail his industrial strategy before it gets going.

Japan’s big bazooka spending programme was meant to do what Mr Burnham now says Britain must do on a smaller scale: use the state to rebuild productive capacity , reduce strategic dependence and build its export competitiveness. Tokyo has the fiscal firepower, a central bank able to dominate the sovereign bond market and trillions invested overseas. The UK government could mimic that and change its fiscal rules, its relationship to the Bank of England and the way investment is accounted for.

But Japan is Mr Burnham’s problem writ large. The war in Iran made it urgent to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. But the conflict’s inflationary shock makes that objective harder – though not impossible – to pursue. Mr Trump’s team is using its leverage over the yen to restrain Tokyo’s plan to make Japan resilient to external price spikes. Mr Burnham has been forewarned: the Gulf inflation shock wave bolsters the argument for economic independence while making the means of achieving it more difficult.

stories.body:
Ahead of a crucial budget, four countries’ experiments offer a mixed verdict on how to tax bumper profits

T he countdown is on. Two months out from Andy Burnham’s inaugural autumn budget, bank executives are wringing their hands over whether the government will target their bumper profits with fresh taxes.

The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly considering a windfall tax on both banks and oil companies in the late October Westminster setpiece.

The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years, largely off the back of rising interest rates .

They are now in the crosshairs of campaigners – including the Trades Union Congress (TUC) and campaign group Positive Money – who say a tax increase could help cover rising household bills as part of Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living.

The TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, who has been pushing hard for a new bank tax said: “Britain’s largest banks are making a fortune. Not because they’ve suddenly become more competitive or improved their services to customers, but because high interest rates mean that, right now, they can sit back and watch the money roll in. Inflated mortgages are fuelling record bonus pots.

“With energy bills edging towards record highs this winter, the government is going to need to provide more support for households – and taxing banks’ windfall profits is the obvious way to pay for it.”

Any move in the UK would echo similar efforts in mainland Europe to make lenders pay more tax to help offset surging living costs and higher defence spending. Here are some of the tools different governments used, as well as the benefits and pitfalls of targeting the profits of some of the world’s largest banks.

Spain: taxed and undeterred

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, revealed plans for a windfall tax in 2022 that would raise €3bn from banks over the following two years to help alleviate cost-of-living pressures.

It spooked investors, wiping more than €5bn off the value of Spanish-listed bank stocks, but politicians pushed ahead: putting a 4.8% “solidarity tax” on the domestic revenue of banks whose income passed €800m. That included fees and net interest income, – the amount of money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits.

The €800m threshold and the focus on domestic revenues meant it broadly excluded small local banks and most foreign lenders’ Spanish operations.

Big banks and lobby groups filed legal challenges over the tax, while the European Central Bank (ECB) warned that Spain risked disrupting monetary policy, and damaging lenders’ capital positions, which help to cushion the blow of economic shocks.

Politicians eventually decided to extend the levy a further three years to 2027, after successfully raising €1.3bn in the first year, and €1.7bn in 2024 . Banks now face a sliding tax rate of between 1% and 7%, with the highest rate hitting lenders such as Banco Santander whose annual revenue from interest and fees surpassed €5bn.

The extension triggered a fresh spate of legal challenges by banks and lobbyists, and criticism from both the International Monetary Fund and ECB, which warned it could hit bank profits , push up borrowing costs for low-income households, and make Spain’s banks less competitive on the international stage.

Lithuania: a defence spending boost

Lithuania’s government decided to roll out its own windfall tax on banks in 2023, after forecasts showed lenders were due to rake in €1.3bn in net profits that year. That was three times higher than 2022, following a surge in interest rates sparked by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The 60% tax, which applied to any net interest income that was 50% higher than the previous four-year average, was used to fund infrastructure projects and boost defence spending amid Russian threats.

Politicians agreed to exclude income from any newly agreed loans, to prevent a situation where banks stopped issuing mortgages and business loans to avoid paying tax.

The levy helped raise about €250m in 2023 and €247m in 2024 , representing 0.3% of the country’s annual GDP, before being extended by an extra year. The European Commission appeared to support the move, saying it helped cut public debt at a time of regional security threats.

But the tax is said to have spooked foreign firms, with the central bank having repeatedly tried to lure new lenders “with no significant success”, according to an EU report.

The banking sector said it also disadvantaged lenders serving local customers, while letting others such as Revolut, which is registered in the country but serves mostly non-residents, off the hook.

Czechia: ‘unrealistic expectations’

Czechia announced its own three-year windfall tax on banks to help cover consumers’ soaring electricity and gas prices in 2022. The temporary measure, lasting from 2023 to 2025, involved a 60% tax on any profits that were more than double (120%) the previous four-year average.

Deeply unpopular with businesses, the tax also caused friction within the far-right ODC civic democratic party , which said it was interfering with the free market and contradicted core conservative values.

Czech finance minister, Zbyněk Stanjura, talked about scrapping the tax a year earlier than planned, but later admitted the levy had not yet covered state costs linked to the energy crisis. While the finance ministry originally hoped to collect more than 30bn Czech koruna from the country’s six largest banks, it quickly became clear they would fall short of those targets.

“It is unclear whether this was due to unrealistic expectations driven by a vision of easy extra revenue and convenient scapegoating of big corporations, or whether the delayed implementation of the tax (from 2022 to 2023) and the behavioural responses by businesses were not duly considered,” the law firm A&O Shearman said in a 2024 report.

The country ended up raising just 1bn Czech koruna, months before the tax expired in December 2025, according to figures reported by local broadcaster Ct24 .

Italy: a tax that fell flat

While plans for a windfall tax by prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing government gained international attention , it was one of the least effective levies.

Meloni’s team shocked markets in August 2023 after revealing plans for a 40% tax on banks’ net interest margin. The move drew the ire of banking lobby groups and wiped €10bn off shares in financial services companies, forcing politicians to water down the proposal a day later with a cap that halved the estimated tax takings to €2.5bn, from €4.9bn.

The rules eventually came into force in October that year, but not before being diluted further.

Banks – which are already subject to higher corporation and regional taxes in Italy – were allowed to choose one of two options: pay a tax equivalent to 0.26% of the risky assets on their balance sheets – ensuring those with safer loans paid less – or keeping the money on their balance sheets but putting aside two-and-a-half times that amount into their own reserves to cushion the blow of any economic shock.

Unsurprisingly, all banks chose to put the money in reserve, scuppering original hopes that extra funds could help support mortgage holders and cut taxes.

However, Italy’s deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, has now revived plans for a new tax three-year levy , that would involve a 5% tax on the profits of Italy’s 10 largest banks.

What if the UK followed suit?

If current trends continue, the UK’s four largest banks will rake in £60bn in profits for 2026. Windfall taxes have been used on banks in the UK before , notably in the early 1980s when Margaret Thatcher’s then chancellor, Geoffrey Howe, accused high street banks of escaping the recession and in the 1990s by Labour chancellor Gordon Brown to generate extra revenue.

Calculations by campaign group Positive Money suggest that the UK could raise up to £10.9bn this year from adopting Czechia’s model; up to £6.95bn by following Spain’s sliding tax scale; and £2.2bn by following in Lithuania’s footsteps.

“Plenty of countries have successfully taxed banks’ windfall profits,” the TUC’s Nowak said. “We’re calling for an increase in the bank surcharge to raise billions for the Treasury to cut bills across the country. This is an easy win for government – and the chancellor should ask the banks to pay a fairer share”.

The world’s most powerful banker, JP Morgan boss, Jamie Dimon, has repeatedly warned the UK government against increasing taxes on banks.

“Banks based here already pay a corporation tax surcharge and the bank levy, giving them a higher total tax rate than in other major financial centres. Increasing sector‑specific taxes would risk damaging the UK’s international competitiveness and make it harder to attract investment.”

We round up this year’s winners at awards for achievements that ‘first make people laugh and then make them think’

It’s that time of year again: a select group of scientists have been summoned to a ceremony to receive coveted prizes, be showered in paper planes, and leave with a 10tn dollar bill, albeit in the form of a phased-out note from Zimbabwe. It is, of course, the annual Ig Nobel awards.

Not to be confused with the more prestigious and career-changing Nobel prizes that will be announced in Scandinavia next month, the satirical Ig Nobels are awarded for achievements that “first make people laugh and then make them think”.

On Thursday, real Nobel laureates were on stage to hand out the awards and winners were giving “24/7” lectures: describing their work in 24 seconds and then in seven words. Here are the 2026 winners.

1. Economics: evil rich people Are rich people really worse behaved than the rest of us? Through a series of experiments, psychologists amassed evidence that the upper classes are indeed more prone to behaving badly, from being oblivious to other road users, lying at work and taking treats meant for children. “I’ve followed the Ig Nobels since my early college days. I didn’t think I’d ever win one,” said Dr Paul Piff, a social psychologist at the University of California, Irvine. Piff and his colleagues found that upper-class drivers were more likely to cut other cars off at junctions and ignore pedestrians at crossings. Wealthier people also appeared more willing to lie at work. In one experiment, volunteers were left alone with a jar of sweets ostensibly meant for children. When the researchers returned, upper-class people had snaffled nearly twice as many candies as lower-class people. “The general pattern seems to be that with wealth and rising power, you become less engaged with the needs of others and less burdened by the needs of social relationships,” Piff said. “Taking candy from children might be the least of our worries but it’s emblematic of the tendency to prioritise one’s own needs over those of others.”

2. Biomechanics: the definition of kissing Researchers at Oxford University ensured the UK could hold its head high after winning the biomechanics prize. “The whole team is thrilled,” said Dr Matilda Brindle. She and her colleagues investigated the evolution of kissing and needed a scientific definition of the act. They settled on “non-agonistic interactions involving directed, infraspecific oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer”. Brindle, who is writing a book on non-reproductive sexual behaviour, has also studied the evolution of masturbation , making her a strong contender to become the Marie Curie of Ig Nobels by winning more than once. “We’re so focused on penises, what they do and why they are important, but all these other sexual behaviours are important,” she said.

3. Physics: The splashless urinal A team of students led by Kavee Thurairajah at the University of Waterloo in Canada worked out that urinal splash is almost entirely eradicated if the stream strikes the urinal at less than 30 degrees. They went on to design a urinal whose shape ensures minimal splash regardless of the user’s aim. “I am very proud,” said Dr Zhao Pan, who runs the lab. View image in fullscreen Researchers at Canada’s University of Waterloo designed an optimal urinal (not pictured). Photograph: Mevans/Getty Images

4. Peace: The power of mutual enemies It is natural to want friends that are kind to us, but our friends interact with others in the world in ways that can affect our lives. Dr Jaimie Krems at the University of California, Los Angeles, showed there’s plenty of room for attack dogs in our friendship groups, as long as they target those we dislike. “Sometimes we want our friends to be more vicious and indifferent when they interact with our enemies,” she said. “I’ve felt, in many instances, incredibly loved when people have carried my hate for me and been willing to have my back.”

5. Biology: The science of stepping on snakes Researchers in Brazil donned safety boots to explore what made venomous snakes bite in defence by softly stepping on different parts of their bodies. Pressure on the head triggered most bites, they had found, but the study had been retracted by the Scientific Reports journal as the team did not have ethical approval to step on the creatures.

6. Ig notable mentions The chemistry prize went to an international team that found cockroach milk contains three times as much energy as cows’ milk, while the olfaction prize went to scientists who discovered babies smell wonderful to their parents, but teenagers do not. Other researchers landed prizes for turning mosquito proboscises into 3D printing nozzles, clarifying the aerodynamics of nose blowing, and burying underpants to monitor soil quality.

stories.title: Burnham to tackle 'mega-donors' in UK politics, minister says
stories.summary: Some MPs have pressed for the government to introduce a cap on UK-based donors.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 3 September 2026, 01:44 BST

Andy Burnham's government is "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors" in UK politics, a minister has said in response to calls for an immediate cap on donations.

Florence Eshalomi said a new team would be "working at pace to find a solution", as some MPs expressed concerns over the influence of wealthy individuals donating large sums of money.

The Labour government has already committed to a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, but ministers have been pressed to go further by introducing a limit for UK-based donors.

Reform UK's Danny Kruger warned the Representation of the People Bill was a "flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap" the party.

Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference Published 17 hours ago

Labour MPs seek cap on political donations Published 3 July

New rules won't stop me donating, says billionaire Reform backer Published 30 April

Reform has been critical of measures contained in the bill and the impact they could have on funding the party receives from donors .

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties and politicians.

Labour MP Stella Creasy said donations from individuals and companies giving £1m or more had "surged" in the last decade and gave examples for different political parties.

Among those she named was British billionaire Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based businessman, who is one of Reform's biggest backers.

Last year he gave a single donation of £9m to Reform - the biggest single donation to a UK political party by a living person.

Creasy was among those who tabled amendments seeking to also impose a cap on UK-based donors.

One of her proposals called for an immediate £500,000 limit which would reduce to £100,000 in the second calendar year. Minsters would have been able to set a permanent cap.

The amendment, which was not moved to a vote, was signed by more than 60 MPs.

Creasy told the Commons: "Obscene wealth is increasingly dictating who is heard, whether we like it or not, what issues are being prioritised and whose interests shape policy decisions."

The Walthamstow MP added that there was a "need to act now to protect the next general election". Her proposals would have exempted trade unions from the donation cap, with the MP saying this is "already well regulated" and "clean money".

Kruger highlighted the millions of pounds donated by trade unions to the Labour Party as he criticised the proposals and the bill.

The MP for East Wiltshire said: "The claim is made that this bill will defend democracy, but actually it's a flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap Reform UK."

The former Conservative MP added: "The suggestion is made that this bill will restore trust in politics and that is exactly what is needed.

"But what they all mean is to restore trust in the class of politicians and in the political parties that have got us into the mess that we are in, including the party I'm afraid to say I was part of which is why I left it. We need change."

Responding for the government, Eshalomi said the bill "already contains a package of significant measures designed to strengthen the political finance regime whilst ensuring that legitimate donors can continue to fund election campaigns".

The communities minister added that the prime minister was among those "determined to tackle the UK-based issue of mega-donors in UK politics".

"That is why I'm happy to commit and announce the new cross-government task and finish team will be working at pace to find a solution without unintended consequences," Eshalomi said.

"I can reassure members that once these solutions have been found, we would want them in force as soon as possible."

Full details of the new team's remit have yet to be confirmed by the government.

It last month emerged that Burnham registered accepting £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.

The Liberal Democrats proposed establishing a royal commission to make recommendations for a cap on political donations and the "effectiveness" of existing campaign expenditure limits.

This proposal was rejected in the Commons by 427 votes to 85, majority 342.

Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said Creasy had made a "clear case" for a cap on all donations, adding she would prefer it to be lower and suggested £50,000 a year.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said it was a "noble aim" to protect UK democracy from foreign influence but changes proposed by the government had not always been produced with "proper care and attention".

In March, the government said donations in cryptocurrency to UK political parties would be banned alongside the move to cap donations of British citizens living abroad at £100,000 annually.

Ministers later announced overseas voters moving to the UK would be prevented from giving more than £100,000 in political donations for a year after their arrival.

This was announced alongside tougher checks on company donations, which they believe will help stop foreign money from influencing UK elections.

The bill also contains measures to change the voting system, including extending the right to vote to 16- and 17-year-olds.

MPs approved the bill at third reading by 411 votes to 102, majority 309, and it will undergo further scrutiny in the House of Lords at a later date.

stories.title: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge
stories.summary: The PM said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as he faced Kemi Badenoch at Prime Minister's Questions for the first time.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 September 2026

Andy Burnham said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as his first Prime Minister's Questions took place against a backdrop of rising UK borrowing costs.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to say where spending would be cut and how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high on Wednesday.

He blamed the previous Tory government, saying the "turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they left behind".

Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July before Parliament's summer recess, meaning Wednesday was the first time he had faced Badenoch at PMQs.

Burnham sought to stress his administration's fiscal responsibility and said ministers were taking steps to reduce debt.

He told MPs: "This will be a government grounded in fiscal responsibility. It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost-of-living pressure on our constituents, and that's the approach that we will take."

Interest rates on government bonds have been going up, with the yield on a 10-year bond at its highest level since 2008, while the yield on a 30-year bond is at its highest since 1998.

This means it costs the government more to borrow over the long term and could constrain its spending choices as the 28 October Budget approaches.

Burnham's PMQs debut came after he used the summer recess to tour the UK, announcing a series of eye-catching policies mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.

On Wednesday, Badenoch said the prime minister had set out plenty of spending plans but no detail of how he would be paying the bill.

"The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from," she said.

"He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice - higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts.

"Yesterday he said change begins with honesty, so will he be honest and tell us: is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?"

Burnham had earlier said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and a cut in business rates for hospitality.

"I've already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I'm not going to do what any prime minister has done and write the budget here," he said, adding he and Chancellor John Healey had agreed on an earlier date for the Budget to reduce speculation.

In the Commons, Badenoch also raised comments from economist and cross-bench peer Lord Jim O'Neill, who had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser, but who ruled out joining Burnham's government .

Speaking to the BBC, Lord O'Neill had praised the PM for "a great first five weeks" which he said had helped lift consumer and business confidence; adding the current spike in market interest rates for government debt would force Labour to start "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Badenoch pointed to a warning from Lord O'Neill that the prime minister's tone during his Tuesday Commons debut would have unsettled investors, although the peer had also said that spike was mostly mirroring US market upheaval concerning the Iran conflict.

Kemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons at PMQs

"Lord O'Neill, a close friend of the prime minister, said yesterday's statement in the Commons was the last thing investors wanted to hear," Badenoch said.

"Lord O'Neill is a serious economist. He knows what he's talking about and, sure enough, yesterday the cost of government borrowing rose to its highest in 18 years.

"How does he plan to tackle the government's rising debt costs?"

Burnham replied that he and Lord O'Neill did "not always agree", before attacking Badenoch's shadow cabinet reshuffle for bringing MPs who were in the leadership team of former Conservative prime minister Liz Truss back to her front benches.

To shouts of "point-scoring!" from the Conservative side, he said: "Can I also say to her and the whole of her new shadow cabinet, the majority of whom were part of a government that lasted for 49 days, a short-lived government that crashed confidence in the economy and hammered people's mortgages.

"She took a decision at the weekend, she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini budget was a mistake, and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped to write the Truss mini budget."

In the Tory reshuffle , Andrew Griffith replaced Sir Mel Stride as shadow chancellor.

Badenoch said Burnham had not ruled out tax rises, claiming: "The reason why that budget failed was because spending was announced before the money to pay for it, which is exactly what he is doing right now."

Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics Published 1 day ago

Why are UK borrowing costs rising and what does it mean for me? Published 1 day ago

Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services Published 1 day ago

The opposition leader went on to raise the alleged Russian attack on Leipzig airport in Germany , urging the prime minister to commit to 3% spending.

So far the new government has only committed to meeting the 3.5% spending target for defence by 2035, pushing back the interim 3% spending commitment to spring next year.

The new chancellor quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, which proved to be the final nail in the coffin for Sir Keir's premiership.

Burnham told MPs: "The very reason I appointed this Chancellor to his position is because of his strong commitment to the defence of our country and to defence spending.

"We will fully fund the defence investment plan and at the spending review we will set out a plan to meet the Nato commitments by 2035, there is no problem with our commitment to defence."

Wong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China

Joshua Wong , one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.

Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.

The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China.

The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.

Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.

In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.

Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.

Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.

Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.

One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings.

“Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.”

In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.

In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.

Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.

“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.

Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.

“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.

“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.

On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”

stories.body:
Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers

Nepal-Tibet floods – latest updates

Visual guide: How the Nepal-Tibet flash flood unfolded

Nepali rescuers have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue hundreds of trapped workers, as the death toll passed 1,000 nearly ⁠a week after devastating ​floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys.

About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts. The prime ⁠minister, Balendra Shah, said more than 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas.

“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” Shah said.

Six days after the catastrophe struck the Himalayan border region, 4,400 people were still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist identification efforts.

In a statement posted to social media, Nepal police on Monday asked relatives of those missing to “provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the Nepal police hospital in Kathmandu, or the nearest district police office.

Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.

Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.

In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues .

At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.

Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.

“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.”

She was waiting for her two other siblings, who live in the UK, to arrive on Tuesday so they could all try to get up to the village. She said she wanted to contact her grandmother or sister-in-law, who she thinks both survived the flood because their house is further up the mountain. Their village was still in a blackout, and making contact was impossible.

“I can’t go there; the situation is very bad,” she said. “I can’t go up there alone. I am not sure if we’ll be able to get them.”

The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse that sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud through Nepal’s border region with China , posing a massive challenge for the country’s six-month-old government.

The region is vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events such as intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.

In a late-night social media post, Shah said aid worth more than $42m had poured into the country, but that Nepalis were reeling. “The government understands the ​immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to ‌support them through this suffering and help ‌them return to normal life through rehabilitation,” the prime minister said.

Shah also said that 279 workers had so far been rescued from hydropower projects, where authorities estimated close to 1,000 people had been trapped. Days after the disaster, hope was rapidly diminishing that any of those trapped in a series of tunnels could be alive.

Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.

Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state broadcaster said on Monday.

Shah said the ​catastrophic event signalled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces. “The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” he wrote in his post.

Swap rates rise to three-year high as increase in oil prices leads to fears of higher inflation

Business live – latest updates

Homeowners in the UK are braced for a jump in mortgage rates, driven by higher inflation and interest rate increase expectations amid turmoil in the global bond markets.

UK swap rates, which lenders use to price mortgages, have risen to a three-year high, as this week’s global bond market sell-off ripples through the economy.

The five-year swap rate rose above 4.52% this week, the highest level since October 2023. This is expected to result in higher interest rates on fixed-term mortgages.

A jump in oil prices as the US and Iran exchanged fire this week for the first time in a month has led to fears of higher inflation, leading investors to sell bonds, which pushes up their yield, or interest rate. The moves in gilts, as UK government bonds are known as, have been bigger than those in other countries.

Coventry Building Society has become the first mainstream lender to increase mortgage rates. It raised rates across its entire range of fixed-rate mortgages for new and existing residential and buy-to-let borrowers.

Although the turmoil in the bond markets eased on Thursday, the consequences of the jump in bond yields could be serious for borrowers.

That is because UK swap rates – the interest rates that banks charge when they borrow from each other – have been pushed up by the rise in gilt yields.

Markets are not expecting the Bank of England to raise interest rates at its policy meeting later this month, though its chief economist, Huw Pill, used a speech on Thursday to underscore his argument for higher rates.

In a speech in Edinburgh, Pill argued: “We cannot wait for uncertainties to resolve themselves before acting.”

Rather than taking a “wait and see” approach, as the Iran war pushes up on inflation, he said, “I see benefit in acting clearly, promptly and decisively … This would cut through the noise inherent in the current uncertain environment in a way that bolsters the clarity and effectiveness of our policy choices.”

Pill was among three members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee to call for a rate rise in July, but they were outvoted.

Russ Mould, the investment director at the trading platform AJ Bell, said: “Credit card, mortgage and auto loan interest rates will rise if bond yields rise, as the lenders seek to preserve loan book margins and manage their risk.”

If the cost of government borrowing continues to remain high, it could undermine Andy Burnham’s efforts to ease cost of living pressures.

after newsletter promotion

The new prime minister attempted to calm volatile bond markets on Wednesday, using his first appearance at prime minister’s questions to promise decisions for the autumn budget would be “grounded in fiscal responsibility”.

He spoke as the yield on UK 10-year government debt hit its highest level since 2008 for a second day, before retreating thanks to a drop in the oil price. On Thursday, Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dipped 0.6% to $95 a barrel.

Oil has been one of the key factors driving the bond market sell-off, as inflationary pressures from high prices could force central banks to raise interest rates, along with worries over high government spending. Government bonds are also competing with a flurry of corporate debt issuance by technology companies keen to fund their spending on AI infrastructure.

Tom Simpson, the managing director of homes at Yorkshire Building Society, said swap rates were now 0.7% above where they were a year ago, but there was “much more volatility” in March, at the start of the Iran war.

“All things being equal, you would expect a modest increase in mortgage rates based on what we’ve seen so far,” he told the BBC, advising people who were worried about this to speak to an independent mortgage adviser.

“When there is a movement in the market, that can pull forward demand. People will try to lock those rates in.” However, he added that the 0.1 percentage point increase over the past week was below the 0.5 percentage point increase in the 10 days after the US and Israel first launched airstrikes on Tehran.

Fixed-year mortgage rates were unchanged on Thursday, according to the latest figures from Moneyfacts. The average two-year fix is 5.59%, while a typical five-year fixed deal costs 5.63%.
